judgments.catchwords: whether a debt financing agreement in the form of a “whole turnover agreement”, had breached s 5(1) of the Moneylenders Act 1951 (MA). A whole turnover agreement between a financier (X) and borrower (Y) provides for - (1) X to advance money to Y with Y’s assignment to X of all of Y’s “future receivables” or Y’s future book debts (Y’s Assignment); and (2) Y’s Assignment shall take effect on a date stated in the whole turnover agreement which is - (a) before Y has issued any invoice to Y’s debtor(s); (b) before Y’s receivables are due to be paid to Y; and (c) before any debt has accrued in favour of Y and is payable to Y. A whole turnover agreement is also known as a “receivables purchase agreement”, “whole turnover factoring” and “whole turnover invoice discounting”.

judgments.title: EXTRA EXCEL (MALAYSIA) SDN BHD v QUEK PECK KEOW
judgments.catchwords: Section 10(1) of the Arbitration Act 2005 - whether section 10(1) of the AA 2005 required the courts below to determine for themselves the existence and operability of the arbitration agreement, or whether that question ought to have been left to the arbitral tribunal under section 18 and the doctrine of kompetenz-kompetenz - whether the 2nd Stay Application and OS 2 are barred by res judicata or issue estoppel arising from the April 2022 Decision - the proper construction of Clause 1.3 in its November 2019 form, and in particular whether it ever entitled the Appellant to commence arbitration against its own distributor - whether the June 2021 amendment to Clause 1.3 could, consistently with ordinary contractual principles, be applied retrospectively to a dispute that had already crystallised and was already the subject of litigation - whether the Appellant had, in any event, taken a step in the proceedings within the meaning of section 10(1), disentitling it to a stay - whether Clause 1.3 is void, in whole or in part, under sections 24 and 29 of the Contracts Act 1950, because it caps the Respondent’s recoverable damages - whether the Appellant’s unilateral right to appoint the sole arbitrator renders the arbitration agreement void, or offends natural justice - whether the finding that the Appellant acted in bad faith was properly made without a trial.

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya v YOU CHIN LOON
judgments.catchwords: CRIMINAL LAW: Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 — Section 39B(1)(a) — Trafficking in dangerous drugs — 777.01 grams of Methamphetamine — Elements of offence — Physical custody and control — Whether prosecution proved actual possession and knowledge beyond reasonable doubt — Competing versions of recovery — Drugs found on sidewalk versus pre-planted in motorcar — Benefit of doubt. CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Trial — Defence case — Standard of proof at conclusion of whole case — Criminal Procedure Code, s. 182A(1) — Maximum evaluation of evidence — Test in Mat v. Public Prosecutor and Public Prosecutor v. Mohd Radzi bin Abu Bakar — Two competing inferences arising from proven facts — Duty of court to draw inference favourable to accused. EVIDENCE: Investigation — Failure of investigating officer to investigate material line of defence — Seized motorcar parked in police station compound left unsearched and uninspected — Failure to forensically examine and extract digital communications from seized mobile phones — Accused alleging entrapment and debt settlement by third party — Deprivation of opportunity to present exculpatory real and digital evidence — Maria Elvira Pinto Exposto v. Public Prosecutor and Rahmani Ali Mohamad v. Public Prosecutor applied — Fatal investigative omissions. EVIDENCE: Witnesses — Credibility — Police witnesses — Presumption of reliability under Public Prosecutor v. Mohamed Ali — Whether presumption absolute — Azrol Nizam Mohd Zaid v. Public Prosecutor applied — Direct conflict between police version and defence testimony — Minor typographical discrepancies in witness statement (Exhibit PSSP3) distinguished from fatal investigative omissions — Evaluation under Amri Ibrahim & Anor v. Public Prosecutor. EVIDENCE: Cross-examination — Rule of put-case — Ayoromi Helen v. Public Prosecutor — Accused’s narrative of third-party entrapment actively challenged by Deputy Public Prosecutor — Whether doctrine of implied acceptance applied — Whether defence a recent fabrication or afterthought — Defence put to prosecution witnesses at earliest opportunity during prima facie stage. EVIDENCE: Real evidence — Search list (Borang Bongkar, Exhibit P4) — Omission of seized vehicle and mobile phones from search list — Failure to take contemporaneous photographs of drugs inside cardboard box at scene of discovery (Exhibit P7) — Reasonable doubt cast on locus and genesis of seizure.

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v Julasiri Bin Akilmara
judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case

judgments.title: LDP PROMOTION FAIR SDN. BHD. v CLOUPOR TECHNOLOGY SDN. BHD. & ors
judgments.catchwords: Tenancy Agreement – Fixed term lease; landlord’s claim for arrears, utilities, restoration costs; tenant’s counterclaim for restitution and damages. Repudiation vs Rescission – Distinction between wrongful repudiation (termination de futuro) and rescission ab initio; prospective termination preserves accrued rights. Misrepresentation – Alleged oral representations; chronological impossibility; doctrine of merger extinguishing independent misrepresentation claims once incorporated into contract. Contracts Act 1950, s.19 & s.74 – Section 19: voidability for misrepresentation subject to diligence exception; Section 74: damages for breach including future rental losses. Ordinary Diligence Exception – Tenant’s failure to verify municipal records and licensing status; experienced entrepreneur held to higher diligence standard. Partial Failure of Consideration – Occupation and renovation for over a year; substantial benefit received; bars restitution under Section 66. Illegality & Pleadings – Procedural bar under Order 18 Rule 8; illegality must be pleaded; “illegal structure” defence raised only in submissions rejected. Excise Act 1976, s.20(1) – Tenant compounded for unlicensed manufacture of excisable goods; statutory breach disentitles reliance on misrepresentation or illegality. Clean Hands Doctrine – Tenant’s unlawful conduct bars equitable relief; cannot seek rescission while implicated in statutory offence. Writ of Distress – Validity under Distress Act 1951; executed within statutory window; lawful recovery of arrears; counterclaim for seized assets rejected. Occupation Principle – Tenant liable for rent during actual occupation notwithstanding alleged illegality; cases distinguished: SSN Medical Products, L’Escargot Cafe. Restitution under s.66 – Partial failure of consideration fatal to claim for full refund; restitution denied to prevent unjust enrichment. Evidence Act 1950, s.114(g) – Adverse inference argument rejected; sufficient witnesses called; no suppression of material evidence. CCTV Evidence – Footage disproved tenant’s “lockout” narrative; showed continued access and asset removal; credibility undermined. Guarantor Liability – Second Defendant bound under guarantee and indemnity; joint and several liability for tenant’s default.
judgments.judge: YA Puan Shoba Rajah a/p Dorai Rajah

judgments.catchwords: Trust - action for breach of trust arising from a trust deed, which has resulted in the Plaintiffs being deprived of their rightful beneficial shares in the proceeds from the sale of the land described in the instrument Photocopy document - secondary evidence in the form of photostat copies is admissible once the court is satisfied that a sufficient search has been conducted and the original documents cannot be found Trust elements - for a private express trust to be perfectly constituted, the ‘three certainties’, namely, certainty of intention, certainty of subject matter, and certainty of object, must be clearly established - a trust obligation is not extinguished by the death of a trustee, rather, it devolves upon his legal representatives or successors in title who take the property subject to the trust. Limitation Act 1953 - operation of s. 22(1)(b) hinges upon two essential prerequisites - first, the existence of a valid trust, and second, that the trust property or its proceeds remain in the possession of the trustee or were previously received and converted to its use Irrevocable power of attorney - contains an express declaration of irrevocability - although no monetary or tangible consideration passed between the parties, the fundamental purpose of the instrument was to empower the children to vindicate and protect their mother’s beneficial rights in the trust property - in the context of a familial proxy born out of physical necessity, that the absence of commercial consideration does not invalidate the mandate

judgments.title: SIVACHANDRAN A/L S JAYARAJAH v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: Review jurisdiction - Rule 137 of the Rules of the Federal Court 1995 -Inherent powers of Federal Court – All sentences passed to be in accordance with the law – Avoiding miscarriage of justice - Exceptional circumstances - Fresh evidence of prisoner’s death following whipping. Constitutional Law - Federal Constitution - Articles 5(1), 8(1) and 8(2) Fundamental liberties - Life and personal liberty - Human dignity - Equal protection of the law - Whether it is in violation of medical ethics for medical officer to be participate in the execution of whipping. Judicial whipping - Corporal punishment - Whether judicial whipping amounts to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment (“CIDT”) - Whether punishment of whipping is inconsistent with constitutional protection of life, dignity and bodily integrity. Whether whipping is disproportionate and therefore contrary to Article 8(1) - Whether exemption of women from whipping constitutes prohibited discrimination on ground only of gender is contrary to Art 8(2) - Intelligible differentia. Whether whipping is against Art. 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (“UDHR”) and the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration in its prohibitions against CIDT - Whether whipping is against customary international law.

judgments.title: RAMESH A/L RAJARATNAM v Pendakwa Raya & ors
judgments.catchwords: Criminal Justice - Insider Trading - Capital Market and Services Act 2007, s 184,185, 188 (2) (a), 195, 198 (1) (c) (ii) - Charge under s. 188 (2) (a) - disposal of shares while in possession of inside information - credit rating downgrade by rating agency (MARC) - Materiality and Price Sensitivity - Reasonable investor test - information generally available - prior public disclosure of likely bond suspension - whether downgrade already priced into market - statutory defences - knowledge of own intentions - pre-determined trading plan declared prior to existence of inside information - Absence of pecuniary purpose - Shares sold at personal financial loss - Proceeds channeled to company for staff wages, EPF, and corporate survival - whether elements of offence established beyond reasonable doubt - statutory defences raised with credible evidence, inferences of facts and circumstances - displaces case of prosecution - two possible inferences - doubt resolved in favor of the accused - appeal allowed - accused/appellant acquitted and discharged.
